S000033.text: WE MUST ADDRESS THE CLIMATE CRISIS The last 11 years have been the hottest 11 years on record. The last three years have been the hottest three years on record. 2026 will be one of the warmest years on record, and most scientists believe 2027 will be the warmest year in recorded history. This past year, Europe has seen four major heat waves, including the continent’s worst heat wave ever that killed more than 10,000 people. In the United States, three extreme heat waves exposed hundreds of millions of people to dangerous levels of heat. Drought is causing some of the lowest water levels ever seen for reservoirs along the Colorado River, threatening the drinking water of 40 million people. Puerto Ricans are being forced to ration water because of extreme drought. In Europe, some of the continent’s dryest conditions have caused major rivers to run so low that ships are running aground, nuclear power plants are shutting down, and historical artifacts that were previously submerged are being revealed. South Korea is in the midst of a record heat wave — with temperatures reaching 108.5° Fahrenheit, the highest temperature in the country’s history. China, India, Pakistan and Afghanistan are all experiencing torrential rain and flooding. As a result of rising heat levels, we are seeing massive wildfires across the world, including Oregon’s worst wildfire season and fires in Washington state that have forced nearly 65,000 families to evacuate. Europe, France and Spain are experiencing destructive wildfire seasons that have forced more than 330,000 people to evacuate their homes. Portugal, Greece, Italy, Albania, Turkey, Canada, Morocco and Algeria are also experiencing destructive wildfire seasons. This summer alone,Alaska, Louisiana, New York, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia have all seen record rainfall events. We’ve seen 1,000-year floods in Texas, Missouri and New York. Once rare, dangerous flash flooding emergencies are now a regular part of summer for tens of millions of Americans. One might think that, in the midst of all of this, there would be major discussions in Congress as to how best to go forward in addressing this existential crisis. Not the case. Insanely, the president of the United States continues to believe that climate change is a “hoax,” and Republican members of Congress are following their “Great Leader” over the cliff. Sadly, too many Democrats think that speaking out on climate change is “bad politics” and have remained far too silent. That has got to change. The simple truth is that we must forcefully take on the greed of the fossil fuel industry and the stupidity of Trump. C001035.text: Tonight on the Senate floor, I urged my colleagues to support the bipartisan continuing resolution I worked with members of both parties to craft as Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. After three unnecessary lapses in funding during the fiscal year 2026 cycle, putting the possibility of yet another harmful government shutdown off the table should be a priority for each and every one of us. This straightforward measure would keep the government funded through December 11, protect vital programs and services, and give Congress additional time to continue our work on bipartisan appropriations bills. We cannot allow another damaging shutdown to disrupt the lives of federal workers and the Americans who depend on their work.

Despite tight personal budgets, it is truly remarkable how often teachers in Maine and across the country use money out of their own pockets to purchase classroom supplies for their students. We are fortunate to have so many dedicated educators who make sacrifices to help ensure that every child has a learning environment that is safe, welcoming, and enriching. That is why I am proud to announce that the Senate today passed the Supporting Early-Childhood Educators’ Deductions (SEED) Act, a bipartisan bill I introduced with Senator Michael Bennet. The SEED Act would provide tax relief for millions of teachers by expanding the above-the-line $300 educator expense deduction, established for K-12 teachers in 2002, to include pre-K and early childhood educators. As the author of the original educator expense tax deduction for K-12 teachers, I am delighted to help lead this effort to expand this benefit to early childhood educators. We can never thank our teachers enough for all they do to prepare the next generation for success, but the Senate’s passage of this commonsense bill brings us one step closer to providing early childhood educators with well-deserved tax relief.

Today, the Senate unanimously passed my bipartisan bill with Senator Tina Smith to reauthorize the Kay Hagan Tick Act, which we first authored in 2019. Maine reported 4,257 cases of Lyme disease last year – more than three times the number of cases reported just six years ago – and 2026 is projected to set yet another record. This is a record that we do not want to set. Our bill will expand efforts to combat Lyme and other tick-borne diseases while supporting promising work already underway in Maine, including a clinical trial for a human Lyme disease vaccine at the MaineHealth Institute for Research and the University of Maine Tick Lab, where Mainers can submit ticks to be identified and tested for pathogens.

I have carefully reviewed Todd Blanche’s qualifications to be Attorney General. This includes his record and responses to questions from Senators at the Department of Justice Appropriations hearing, his confirmation hearing, and in the weeks that followed. While I believe Mr. Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political. Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation: Mr. Blanche approved an order to shield the President, his sons, and the family business from IRS audits, protections unavailable to other American taxpayers. He approved the creation of a $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund. He promised an anti-abortion organization that he would seek to prohibit the mailing of abortion medication to women nationwide. Under his leadership, the Department attempted to indict Senators Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin over their ill-advised, but constitutionally protected, videos encouraging resistance to unlawful orders. More than 1,200 former Department of Justice employees have opposed his nomination, arguing that he has undermined the institution. For these reasons, I will vote against this nomination.

B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

Next month will mark the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks on 9-11. Nearly 3,000 Americans died that day, including over 400 first responders. 34-year-old Stephen Siller was a firefighter with Brookyln's Squad 1 on September 11th. He'd finished his shift and was headed for the golf course when he first heard about the World Trade Center being struck by an airplane. Without a second thought, he returned to his station, grabbed his gear, and began racing to the scene of an unfolding disaster. When Stephen got to the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, it had already been shut down for security purposes. So he strapped on his 60 pounds of equipment, ran three miles, and made it to the Twin Towers ready to save lives. Stephen was last seen just outside of the South Tower, which collapsed at 9:59 that morning. He left behind a wife and five children. Thank you to the @Tunnel2Towers Foundation for making so many Americans aware of Stephen's sacrifice, and for bringing original artifacts from the World Trade Center here to the heart of the county. It is with heartfelt sadness that I learned of the passing of my dear friend, and magnificent former colleague, Kay Granger of Fort Worth, Texas. Some simply hold the gavel – Kay demonstrated what it meant to wield it. Her life and career were defined by a remarkable legacy of firsts: the first woman to become Mayor of Fort Worth, the first Republican woman elected to Congress from Texas, the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, and the first woman to lead House Republicans on the Appropriations Committee. Yet, Kay never rested in the remarkableness of each milestone – she was always ready for the next responsibility, the next challenge, and the next opportunity to serve. I admired Kay Granger the moment I met her. She carried herself with an unmistakable grace, but behind her regal appearance was a razor-sharp tenacity that commanded any room. Kay demanded respect, and she got it from everyone she ever interacted with. Whip-smart and Texas tough, she had a presence that could settle any debate with little more than a look. I was lucky enough to know her personally and professionally through our work serving together in Republican leadership. So, I can attest with firsthand knowledge that ‘Don’t mess with Texas’ was more than a motto when it came to Kay. I know it well because I lost to her when we both sought the chairmanship of the Appropriations Committee previously. After that, our friendship and mutual respect didn’t change for one another. In fact, she named me to be her Vice Chair. Her mentorship and guidance were large parts of my own committee journey and helped prepare me for the privilege of succeeding her as Chairman. On the Appropriations Committee, Kay was known as a fiscal conservative, a defense hawk, and a hard – but fair – negotiator. Ever proud of her Texas roots, Granger ferociously fought for the interests of the Lone Star State. Her colleagues on both sides of the aisle always respected her professionalism, her good humor, her unfailing civility, and her willingness to strike a deal. Indeed, she and the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Committee, Nita Lowey of New York, were fast friends. They were partners who set the gold standard of how to achieve bipartisan consensus. Their portraits above our dais today remind us of the example they set and the responsibility we inherit. I will miss my friend Kay Granger. She set an unmatched standard of excellence, civility, professionalism, and dedication to duty that few can match – and no one will ever exceed. My thoughts and prayers are with Kay’s family, friends, and many admirers. We have lost a great lioness of the House, and I have lost a dear friend to whom I shall always be indebted.

Today marks #VotingRightsDayOfAction, a day to honor the legacy of the civil rights leaders who fought to protect every American’s fundamental right to vote.  As voting rights continue to face new legal and political challenges, I remain committed to protecting access to the ballot box and every American voter can make their voice heard. Our democracy is strongest when every voice is counted.

Today, we recognize #NationalFarmworkerAppreciationDay and honor the hardworking farmworkers whose dedication helps feed our nation. Here in the San Joaquin Valley, the breadbasket of America, we see firsthand the essential role farmworkers play helping sustain our agricultural economy and putting food on tables across the country. Today and every day, we thank them for their hard work, resilience, and commitment.

81 years ago, the bombing of Hiroshima forever changed history. Today, we pause to remember the lives lost and reflect on our shared responsibility to honor their memory. May we continue to uplift the resilience of Japanese Americans in our Valley and recommit ourselves to ensuring that history is never forgotten, and never repeated.

Central Valley families, hospitals, and health care providers are already feeling the effects of the historic Medicaid and Affordable Care Act cuts under H.R. 1. These cuts are forcing providers to make difficult decisions that could impact access to care for the communities they serve. Yesterday, I welcomed @RepPeteAguilar, Chair of @HouseDemocrats, to the Central Valley to hear directly from health care professionals on the front lines, elevate the challenges they’re facing, and reaffirm our commitment to protecting affordable, accessible health care for families across California and the nation.

C001069.text: Now more than ever, we need to support the next generation of farmers. I’m excited to reintroduce the bipartisan Young Farmer Success Act with @CongressmanGT. Our bill would make full-time farmers eligible for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, incentivizing young people to enter careers in agriculture, creating a pathway for their success, and helping secure America’s farming future.

61 years ago this week, the Voting Rights Act became law, helping to fulfill the promise that every eligible American should have an equal voice at the ballot box. Today, with this hallmark achievement of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and the civil rights movement hanging by a threat, we must recommit to defending the rights of all Americans to participate of in free and fair elections.

The skills training movement is happening in every corner of eastern Connecticut. Yesterday, I visited the first cohort of a new adult welding program at Tourtellotte Memorial High School in Thompson. Under a partnership between the high school and CT State Quinebaug Valley Community College, the welding lab, which opened to students in 2024, will now also be used for adult programs from 8:00 am to 2:30 pm in the summer and 3:30 to 9:30 pm starting in the fall. It’s through collaboration like this that eastern CT will meet the unprecedented demand for skilled manufacturing in the submarine industry.

Thanks to the Northeastern CT Chamber of Commerce for hosting me at “Coffee with the Congressman” in Hampton. We discussed the urgent need to build more quality and affordable homes across eastern CT and the bipartisan “Road to Housing” bill that Congress recently passed into law to clear pathways for housing construction. The new record contract awards to Electric Boat to build nine Virginia-class and five Columbia-class submarines will intensify our region’s housing needs. I was also glad to recognize the outstanding leadership of the Chamber’s Executive Director Elle-Jordyn Sherman, who will depart her role at the end of September. She has been a great partner to local businesses and the entire northeastern CT community.

Summer meals programs provide a critical resource to families and are meeting greater demand today amid the affordability crisis. Yesterday, I visited Putnam Public Schools’ summer meals program. The program, and others like it across our region, are supported by Congress through the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Funded separately from the summer meals program, Interfaith Human Services of Putnam provides funding so parents and guardians who accompany the participating children also receive free meals. Food Service Director Jeanette Courture is working hard to keep kids fed. This program is a real-life example of why continued federal support for meals assistance is so critical.

RT by @RepRickCrawford: 🚨 FBI PSA: Malicious Cyber Actors Targeting Water and Wastewater Sector PLCs The FBI warns that malicious cyber actors are conducting cyber attacks targeting operational technology devices. These threat actors are remotely accessing internet-facing PLCs, changing IPs and passwords, and causing operational disruption, including pressure loss and flooding. Key Protective Measures: ➡️ Disconnect PLCs from the public-facing internet ➡️ Change default passwords ➡️ Restrict network access ➡️ Set physical PLC mode switches to “Run” ➡️ Maintain manual operation capability ➡️ Review PLC project files ➡️ Plan for end-of-life replacements If you or someone you know has sustained similar OT outages, please contact your local FBI field office and file a complaint at http://www.ic3.gov. For full details and guidance: https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/malicious-cyber-actors-targeting-water-and-wastewater-sector-internet--facing-programmable-logic-controllers-causing-operational-disruptions

For 250 years, our great experiment has faltered, flourished, evolved, and progressed. The American experience is ever-changing and as diverse as the people who call this country home. But one thing has remained constant – the idea of America has always been a beacon of hope. Protecting this country and the ideals and values it was founded on takes work. Democracy is demanding. It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. God Bless America always, God Bless all who call her home, and God Bless our courageous men and women in uniform who continue the fight for liberty today.

On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

S001148.text: RT by @CongMikeSimpson: Great day at Idaho National Laboratory, one of America’s most important centers for advancing the nuclear technologies that will power our future on Earth and in space. The progress underway on SR-1 Freedom was especially exciting to see. For more than 60 years, taxpayers have invested billions in space nuclear technology. Yet America has flown just one reactor in space, and it never left Earth orbit. We’re changing that. SR-1 Freedom is our Nautilus. Like the first ship of the Nuclear Navy, it does not need to begin as the perfect end-state system. It needs to fly, establish operating experience, and give us the foundation for increasingly capable reactors and spacecraft that follow. That progress on nuclear energy can ultimately provide dependable power for the Moon Base, enable more ambitious exploration throughout the outer solar system, and help produce the spacecraft that someday carry astronauts to Mars and bring them home safely. NASA should be working on the near-impossible capabilities others are not positioned to pursue. Nuclear power and propulsion in space belongs squarely in that category. Thank you to @GovernorLittle, @CongMikeSimpson, DOE Deputy Secretary James Danly, the entire @INL workforce, and our partners at @ENERGY for the work underway to finally get America moving on nuclear power in space. SR-1 is just the beginning. The Nuclear NASA is coming.

Brown of Siloam Springs. The downing of Extortion 17 is the largest single-incident loss of life during the War in Afghanistan. These men exemplified service and duty, sacrificing their lives in devotion to something greater than themselves—a sacrifice that speaks to their extraordinary level of character and bravery. John Brown and Thomas Ratzlaff’s legacy of courage and selfless service endures in the young men and women—many from Northwest Arkansas—who have sworn an oath to defend the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic. S001195.text: Had a great time visiting Faithful Farming in Howell County this week with Jake and Brittney Long to see the operation behind their online platform and hear how they’re building something to hand down to their sons. Jake’s family has been raising livestock on this farm since right after the Great Depression. His dad ran it as a dairy for 35 years before Jake came home from college and the family shifted to commercial beef cattle, now running about 175 cows. Between his day job as Superintendent of Howell Valley Schools and serving as a pastor, Jake’s up by 4:30 most mornings — and he and Brittney started Faithful Farming to document that life for their boys, Henry and Jack. We also discussed the threats that New World Screwworm and Theileria pose to cattle producers across our district, and I’ll continue fighting to ensure the USDA has the resources it needs to combat both. Thanks to the Working Families Tax Cuts, farms like this one can count on permanent 100% immediate expensing and a permanent small business deduction, giving them the tools to invest, grow their herd, and stay profitable year after year — so this operation can one day be handed down to Henry and Jack. I’ll keep fighting to make sure Missouri farm families have what they need to keep this way of life going.

I got the chance to visit Bahr Farms in St. James this week with Ben Bahr to see the operation their family has built over generations. We discussed the rising cost of fuel, feed, and fertilizer, staffing shortages at USDA’s Farm Service Agency offices, and the challenge of passing their farm on to the next generation. That’s exactly why I fought to make the death tax exemption and small business deduction permanent in the Working Families Tax Cuts, so families like the Bahrs can pass their land down instead of losing it to taxes. I’ll keep pushing for solutions on rising input costs and for stronger USDA support so farmers aren’t stuck driving further just to get basic assistance.

F000466.text: On a six-acre farm just outside New Hope, Jessica Zander has built something our community should be deeply proud of. Helping Friendly Farm in Solebury Township is a place where children, families, and individuals with disabilities can grow, connect, and feel fully welcomed. For more than 20 years, Jessica has devoted her life to individuals with special needs, helping them build confidence, skills, and foster positive opportunities and connection. Her path began with my longtime partners at AmeriCorps, where she served as a special education teacher. From there, she continued serving in specialized mental health and special education programs, and brought therapeutic yoga and meditation to children with special needs. As a mother of children with complex medical needs, Jessica understands what so many families carry every day—the appointments, questions, advocacy, trials and tribulations, and constant search for places where their loved ones will be met with patience, respect, and understanding. So, Jessica created that place. At Helping Friendly Farm, visitors of all ages and backgrounds can pet donkeys, sit with goats, explore a sensory barn, plant seeds, play on swings, spend time in nature, and connect with animals raised to be gentle and familiar with wheelchairs and adaptive devices. It is not clinical. It is not overwhelming. It is warm, intentional, evidence-based, and full of joy, compassion, and a place where all people are seen not for what limits them, but for all they are capable of becoming. Her work reflects the kind of mission I will always fight for: ensuring that children, families, caregivers, and individuals with disabilities are seen, supported, included, and given every opportunity to thrive. Please join me in thanking and applauding Jessica and the entire HFF team for creating such an extraordinary place in our community—a true Hometown hero!

I first met Doylestown’s own Allison Hamilton in Washington last October, when she joined us with The Nature Conservancy to discuss the conservation challenges facing our region. Since then, we have continued working together on several of the conservation priorities most important to our region. Chief among them is protecting the Delaware River. As Co-Chair of the Congressional Delaware River Watershed Caucus, I am leading the bipartisan effort to reauthorize and strengthen the Delaware River Basin Restoration Program—ensuring continued investments in cleaner water, restored habitats, and the local communities and economies that depend on a healthy river system. We are also working together to advance my bipartisan Safeguarding Endangered Species Act, which would overturn the Administration’s rollback of longstanding protections against habitat destruction that kills or injures threatened and endangered wildlife. The health of our environment is inseparable from the health, character, and prosperity of our communities. Allison’s local perspective, The Nature Conservancy’s expertise, and their continued partnership are indispensable to moving this work forward. Thank you to Allison and the entire TNC team for all you do for our community, our environment, and the natural resources entrusted to our care.

When President Lyndon Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act into law on this day in 1965, he enshrined a truth that countless generations before had fought for: no American should be denied a voice in our democracy because of the color of their skin. But progress is never permanent. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court weakened the very heart of this law, and state after state worked around the clock to reverse the protections that took generations to win. Let's be clear: the right to vote is not a partisan idea. It's the foundation of everything we hold near and dear to our hearts. It was won by people who believed America could be better than it was, and it falls on us to defend their legacy. We will keep that promise.

C001129.text: On this day in history in 1782, George Washington created the Purple Heart during his time as the commander in chief of the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War. He awarded it to only three soldiers during the Revolutionary War. The purple badge allowed soldiers to pass guards without challenge and have their names recorded in the “Book of Merit.” The award was forgotten until it was reinstated on Washington’s 200th birthday in 1932. Today, the Purple Heart is awarded to soldiers who have been wounded, killed, or prisoners of war. It is the oldest American award for the armed forces.

On this day in history in 1945, the United States dropped the first atomic bomb on the city of Hiroshima in Japan. The U.S. began developing nuclear weapons in 1940 after learning Germany was doing the same. Although Germany was defeated before the bomb was ready, the war with Japan continued. To avoid heavy U.S. casualties, President Truman ordered the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, killing 80,000 instantly and 60,000 more from fallout. Days later, a second bomb hit Nagasaki. Japan surrendered a week later, ending World War II.

On this day in history in 1926, master illusionist Harry Houdini was submerged underwater in an airtight metal casket after being challenged by rival magician Rahman Bey. It would take Houdini 91 minutes to escape. This was the final major stunt of a career filled with daring escapes and illusions. Three months later, Houdini died at age 52 from complications of a ruptured appendix. He was laid to rest at Machpelah Cemetery in Queens, New York.

D000230.text: Friday in the First April Baker, a Nashville resident and founder and executive director of A Touch of the Father's Love, has spent the past 14 years ensuring that families across eastern North Carolina never have to wonder where their next meal will come from. L000598.text: Today, on National Purple Heart Day, I had the honor of presenting the Purple Heart to U.S. Army Specialist Fourth Class Daniel J. Knote of Riverhead, a Vietnam Veteran whose courage under fire exemplifies the very best of American service. On February 27, 1968, Specialist Knote was shot while moving through enemy fire to rescue a fellow Soldier in Vietnam. Although his heroism earned him the Purple Heart that year, the honor went missing from his official military record for nearly six decades. Thanks to the diligent efforts of my casework team, we located the original order and were able to set the record straight. Helping our nation’s heroes get the recognition they deserve is a privilege, and I was honored to present Specialist Knote with his long-overdue Purple Heart. The Purple Heart is a solemn reminder that freedom has always carried a cost and that courageous Americans have always answered the call to defend it. God bless Daniel, every Purple Heart recipient, and all those who paid a personal price to preserve the freedoms that remain America’s greatest inheritance.

M001228.text: The State of Utah and the U.S. Forest Service are teaming up to provide $18 million to support Beaver County’s recovery.

RT by @RepMaloyUtah: On Pioneer Day, I had the opportunity to tour Beaver and see firsthand the devastating impact of both wildfire and flooding. Standing in those burned and flooded landscapes, talking with the Forest Service personnel, local leaders, and the people of Beaver one thing was crystal clear: forest management works. The difference between treated and untreated forest was visible. Areas that had been thinned or otherwise managed gave firefighters a chance. They slowed the fire, reduced its intensity, helped crews establish containment lines, and in some cases, stopped the fire altogether. In the overgrown, untreated areas, the fire burned hotter, moved faster, and left behind far greater destruction, burning an unprecedented 70,000 acres in two days. It's frustrating that while the United States is the world's largest importer of lumber and paper products, millions of acres of our own forests sit overcrowded and vulnerable to catastrophic wildfire. The boots-on-the-ground Forest Service personnel managing these forests know what needs to be done and want to actively manage these lands, but too often commonsense projects are delayed or stopped by endless litigation and opposition by environmentalists and bureaucrats in Washington D.C. That's why the Fix Our Forests Act deserves to move forward. The legislation passed the House with strong bipartisan support, but has been stalled in the Senate for 18 months. It needs to move forward. I'm grateful to Congresswoman Celeste Maloy for bringing us together to see this firsthand, and to the Trump Administration officials who came to Utah to witness these conditions on the ground. With the U.S. Forest Service headquarters coming to Utah, we have a tremendous opportunity to ensure the people making decisions about our forests are closer to the landscapes and communities they serve. Thank you to USDA's Michael Boren, Sam Crofts from the Bureau of Land Management, and Chairman Bruce Westerman of the House Natural Resources Committee for taking the time to be there and hear directly from those who have been impacted by this catastrophe. On Pioneer Day weekend, that lesson feels especially meaningful. The pioneers who settled this state understood that stewardship requires hard work, planning, and taking responsibility for the land we call home. We honor their legacy not by leaving our forests untouched until they burn and cause catastrophic damage, but by actively caring for them so they remain healthy for generations to come. The Beaver community continues to show incredible resilience. I was reminded why I'm so proud to be a Utahn. We face challenges head-on, we help our neighbors, and we don't shy away from doing the difficult work that's necessary to protect our communities and our public lands. @realDonaldTrump @RepMaloyUtah @RepWesterman @SenJohnCurtis @RepBurgessOwens @RepMikeKennedy @USDA @forestservice @Interior @BLMNational @NatResources @JStuartAdams @cralbrecht52 @BeaverCountyUT

RT by @RepMaloyUtah: Congresswoman Celeste Maloy toured the Cottonwood Fire burn scar in Beaver County today, telling KUTV's Samantha Hoffman the damage is extensive and warning that burn scar flooding remains a major concern for nearby communities. Maloy explained what comes next as local leaders work to assess the damage and begin the process of applying for FEMA grants to help with recovery. She was joined by Sen. John Curtis, House Natural Resources Committee Chairman Bruce Westerman, U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz and Interior Department Senior Adviser Sam Crofts, who discussed Utah's 2026 wildfire season, forest management and efforts to reduce the risk of future catastrophic fires. 🎥 Watch @KUTV2News @samhoffmannews #Utah #BeaverCounty #CottonwoodFire #Wildfire #CelesteMaloy #JohnCurtis #FEMA #FixOurForests

Yesterday, I brought a group to Beaver that doesn't often travel together: members of Congress, state legislators, and Forest Service officials. We walked through neighborhoods destroyed by floods and surveyed the destruction left by the Cottonwood Fire. The damage is widespread and severe, and recovery is going to take time. The people of Beaver are resilient, but resilience shouldn't have to be the plan. Better forest management reduces this kind of risk, and for too long the federal government hasn't listened to the Utahns who know these lands best. That's starting to change, and visits like this one are part of making sure that continues.

ROAD TO 250: The Road to Independence On August 7, 1782, General George Washington established the Badge of Military Merit, the forerunner to today's Purple Heart. Created during the Revolutionary War, it recognized extraordinary acts of valor by American soldiers fighting for our nation's independence. More than two centuries later, the Purple Heart remains one of our nation's most revered military honors. Since its modern revival in 1932, more than 1.9 million service members have received the Purple Heart for being wounded or killed in combat. As a Member of Congress, serving our veterans is one of my highest privileges. I have had the profound honor of presenting a Purple Heart to Corporal Chris Levi of Melville, as well as three posthumous Purple Hearts to the families of Sergeant Leander Willett, Private Julius Schwarz, and Boatswain's Mate Second Class William Olitsky. As we continue to mark America's 250th anniversary, we honor the legacy of courage that began with the soldiers of the Revolution and lives on in every Purple Heart recipient. On Purple Heart Day, we extend our deepest gratitude to all who have sacrificed in defense of our nation.

Exercising your right to worship should not require you to exhibit particular courage as you enter your synagogue, church, mosque, temple, mandir, or gurdwara. That’s why I’m proud to lead this bipartisan and bicameral Right to Worship Act that both protects free speech and the freedom to worship with @RepKnott (R-NC), @SenatorSlotkin (D-MI), and @SenTedCruz (R-TX). https://suozzi.house.gov/media/in-the-news/newsday-suozzi-bill-would-create-buffer-zones-protests-places-worship

B001323.text: Yesterday, I had the opportunity to visit Coast Guard Air Station Sitka and meet with the outstanding men and women who serve on the front lines of Alaska’s @USCG maritime operations. This landmark investment by the U.S. Space Force is a tremendous win for Alaska and America’s national security! The Pacific Spaceport Complex-Alaska in Kodiak is uniquely positioned to support rapid, responsive launch capabilities. I’ve had the opportunity to personally tour our Kodiak spaceport and see firsthand the incredible potential of this facility. It's clear that Alaska offers a strategic advantage few places in the world can match, with the infrastructure and geography to support the next generation of defense and space innovation. As a member of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, I am a continuous advocate for our spaceport. Today’s announcement serves as a reinforcing confirmation of Alaska’s indispensable role in America’s space economy.

This week, I had the opportunity to meet with @NASAAdmin Jared Isaacman to discuss the future of American leadership in space and the critical role Alaska will play in that mission.   As a member of the @housescience Committee, I'm committed to ensuring Alaska has a seat at the table as Congress works to support the future of America's space program.   Our nation is entering a new era of exploration in space, and Alaska is uniquely positioned to help lead the way. We discussed the tremendous potential of the Kodiak Spaceport Complex, one of the nation's critical commercial launch sites, as well as Poker Flat Research Range outside of Fairbanks, the world's only university-owned rocket range and a cornerstone of atmospheric and space research.   As investment in aerospace continues to grow, we have an incredible opportunity to prepare Alaska's students, engineers and technicians for high-paying careers right here at home. By strengthening partnerships with NASA, our universities, our military installations, and the private sector, we can ensure Alaska remains a key player in space innovation.   I appreciate Administrator Isaacman taking the time to discuss our shared vision and look forward to working together to ensure Alaska continues to serve as a vital launch point for discovery and as a key component in our nation's space leadership strategy.

I was honored to welcome my friend, the Ambassador of Hungary to the United States, @_SzabolcsTakacs to Haralson County today. In the late 1800s, dozens of Hungarian families moved from Pennsylvania's coal mines to Haralson County to establish a wine-making community.  They named their village Budapest after the Hungarian capital, and planted vineyards across the surrounding hillsides.  After Prohibition was enacted in the 1920s, many of the families left, and all that remains from that era is a home which once served as a Catholic rectory and the historic Budapest cemetery.  Today, we visited both. Ambassador Takács' visit is a special moment in Haralson County's rich history, and I am grateful for the incredible support the Haralson County Historical Society, the Hungarian Community Church of Georgia, the Dogwood Hills team, and local officials and community leaders provided to facilitate this meaningful event. Thank you, Ambassador Takács, for visiting Georgia's 3rd Congressional District, and thank you for strengthening the relationship between Hungary and the United States of America! @HungaryinUSA

RT by @RepBrianJack: Grateful to join the amazing Steve Gradick of WLPP and @RepBrianJack in Carrollton, Georgia yesterday for a fun long chat on all things America, agriculture, and saving our country. We announced the finalized Cooperative Interstate Shipment (CIS) agreement, giving qualifying Georgia state-inspected meat processors the opportunity to ship USDA-labeled products across state lines. This is a tremendous victory for Georgia's farmers, ranchers, and small meat processors. Yesterday, Georgia became one of only a handful of states participating in the Cooperative Interstate Shipment Program—allowing qualifying state-inspected meat processors to ship USDA-labeled products nationwide. For too long, a handful of massive processors have dominated the market, putting family-owned processors at a disadvantage. This is another step toward expanding opportunity, strengthening rural America, increasing competition, and rebuilding America's food production capacity. Under Biden, the United States flipped from net agricultural exporter to net importer. Four years of weakness turned a historic American strength into a strategic vulnerability. We’re fixing that. Food security is national security. Thank you Georgia!!! 🥩🐂🇺🇸

Today is National Lighthouse Day! Did you know that the Thomas Point Shoal Lighthouse – which has guided mariners for over 150 years – is the only original screw pile lighthouse in the Bay still afloat and alight?  During my time in the Maryland Senate, I worked alongside the keepers of the light, the supporters of the lighthouse, to secure crucial funding to upgrade the substructures and support their hard work in maintenance. In Congress, I’ll always keep fighting for our Bay, our maritime history, and to keep the light shining for another 150 years. As George Bernard Shaw said, “I can think of no other edifice constructed by man as altruistic as a lighthouse. They were built only to serve.”

Today is Purple Heart Day, a time to honor our servicemembers for their bravery in service of our country. The Purple Heart is one of the oldest awards in the military – recognizing those who were wounded or killed in action fighting for our nation and its fundamental values. These brave men and women have made sacrifices most of us can only imagine making for our country. As a member of the House Armed Services Committee, I am proud to represent and honor them and all our active duty servicemembers and veterans today and every day.

From the Coast Guard Yard in #MD03 to the Baltimore Clipper to the production of 384 Liberty ships during World War II, Maryland’s rich maritime history is both storied and bound for a comeback. That’s why at the Masters, Mates & Pilots (@MMP_Union) Conference – hosted right here in Linthicum – I spoke about the importance of reinvesting in our shipbuilding and maritime industries for our national security and diverse economy. Whether it's supporting pro-labor, pro-maritime legislation like the SHIPS for America Act or working directly with our partners at Coast Guard Yard to create new jobs from historic federal investment, I’m proud to stand up for our critical maritime industries so we can be a nation capable of doing big things again.

L’Union européenne et ses partenaires continueront d’accroître la pression sur la Russie, notamment par de nouvelles sanctions, tout en renforçant le soutien militaire à l’Ukraine afin qu’elle puisse se défendre et protéger sa population.

Face à la situation migratoire à Ceuta, j’ai été en contact avec le Président du gouvernement espagnol pour marquer notre solidarité et proposer toute aide nécessaire, y compris via Frontex. Je salue la coopération en cours avec le Maroc, qui a déjà permis aujourd’hui plus de 40 000 retours de Ceuta vers le Maroc. Les ministres de l’Intérieur sont en contact pour assurer un suivi étroit de la situation. Ceuta ne bénéficie pas de la libre circulation vers le reste de l’espace Schengen. J’ai toutefois demandé dès hier au Ministre de l’Intérieur de renforcer les contrôles à notre frontière avec l’Espagne si cela devait être nécessaire : 4 unités de forces mobiles, des avions et des drones sont déployés. Ces mesures viennent renforcer les dispositions que nous avons prises depuis 2020 pour mieux protéger notre frontière avec l’Espagne en étroite coordination, avec des brigades communes et une action conjointe de lutte contre l’immigration clandestine. Ces mesures viennent compléter les instruments européens adoptés pour assurer les retours et appliquer le pacte asile et migrations, avec 25% de chute des flux irréguliers vers l’Union européenne l’an dernier et une baisse poursuivie sur les routes migratoires atlantique et de Méditerranée occidentale en 2026. Solidarité et responsabilité avec nos partenaires européens pour faire appliquer nos règles de fermeté en matière de retours et de protection des frontières extérieures de l’Union. Je redis ici notre solidarité à l’Espagne, son gouvernement et son peuple.
